summary.one_line: Foodlink is India's largest luxury wedding and event caterer, but only on its own paid-for industry report. It has added banquets and a patchy restaurant chain, and it swung to a Rs 16.15 crore consolidated loss in H1 FY27 as its UAE subsidiary bled. The Rs 360.76 crore IPO is 47% OFS. Most of the fresh money goes to sites not yet identified, and the largest slice goes to more UAE restaurants. Avoid at issue.
bull_points: Revenue from operations grew from Rs 377.19 crore in FY24 to Rs 450.86 crore in FY25 and Rs 567.50 crore in FY26, a roughly 23% two-year CAGR. EBITDA margin widened from 8.12% to 13.82% (S2).
The company-commissioned Frost & Sullivan report ranks Foodlink first in FY25 revenue among its organised ultra-luxury and luxury catering peer set, with Rs 343.76 crore of catering revenue (S1).

Bank debt is small. Total borrowings were Rs 22.38 crore against net worth of Rs 216.01 crore at 30 September 2026. Operating cash flow was positive in every reported period, including Rs 44.16 crore in H1 FY27 (S2).

The banquets and integrated F&B business grew from Rs 42.81 crore in FY24 to Rs 127.76 crore in FY26 (11.35% to 22.51% of revenue). That diversifies the company away from pure outdoor wedding catering (S2).
bear_points: Consolidated loss of Rs 16.15 crore in H1 FY27. EBITDA margin collapsed to 7.35%, and the UAE subsidiary FGRCS alone lost Rs 22.70 crore, which the RHP blames on regional conflict (S1, S2).

Rs 50.81 crore of fresh-issue money goes into that same loss-making UAE subsidiary for four new restaurants. The group shut 11 casual dining restaurants and 10 cloud kitchens between April 2023 and the RHP date (S1).
No site, lease or vendor order has been finalised for any capex object: the kitchen, the banquets or the UAE restaurants. Deployment is scheduled for FY28 (S1).
Of the Rs 360.76 crore issue, Rs 168.76 crore (47%) is an offer for sale. The promoter sells about 22.9 lakh shares acquired at a weighted average cost of Rs 0.19 per share (S2, S4).

The Income Tax Department ran a search under section 132 starting 17 December 2025 and seized Rs 1.06 crore in cash. A block-assessment notice covering April 2019 to February 2026 is pending, and the auditors flag it as an emphasis of matter (S1).
watch_points: The outcome of the section 158BC block assessment, for which no order had been issued by the RHP date (S1).
Whether H2 FY27, the peak wedding season, restores full-year profitability after the H1 loss (S2).
Trade receivables doubled from Rs 29.84 crore at FY25 to Rs 60.05 crore at FY26 while revenue grew 26%. Watch cash conversion (S1).
Whether the Rajasthan kitchen and banquet sites and the UAE restaurant sites are identified on schedule (S1).
Day-1 demand was retail-led with QIBs at 0.00x in the morning snapshots. Final QIB participation is the real read on institutional appetite (S10).

reasoning: The use of proceeds does not match the business's own track record. Rs 50.81 crore goes to the UAE subsidiary that lost Rs 22.70 crore in H1 FY27, to open restaurants in a format the group has repeatedly shut (21 outlets closed since April 2023). No location, lease or vendor order is in place for any capex object (S1).

Profitability is fragile and partly flattered. The group made a loss in FY24 (Rs 15.35 crore), a profit in FY25 and FY26, then a loss again in H1 FY27. FY25 and FY26 PAT benefited from net tax credits (total tax of minus Rs 2.23 crore and minus Rs 0.11 crore), so FY25 PAT exceeded PBT (S1).

Cash conversion deteriorated in the best year. FY26 operating cash flow was only Rs 29.91 crore against EBITDA of Rs 78.43 crore (about 38%). Trade receivables doubled to Rs 60.05 crore, and capex plus investing outflows of Rs 59.43 crore exceeded operating cash generation (S1, S2).

There is no structural moat. The 'largest luxury caterer' claim rests on a report the company commissioned and paid for, using a hand-picked unlisted peer set. Catering is word-of-mouth, chef-dependent and relationship-driven, and permanent-staff attrition ran at 51.20% in FY26 (S1).

Governance overhangs are material for a company of this size: an open income-tax search and block assessment, a GST show-cause notice for Rs 23.32 crore, and an older income-tax dispute over Rs 10.45 crore of share-capital additions now at the High Court. Meanwhile the promoter exits part of his holding at a cost of Rs 0.19 per share (S1, S2).

The underlying franchise of event catering plus banquets is real and growing. Revisit the stock after listing if the block assessment closes cleanly, H2 FY27 restores profit and the UAE business stabilises (S2).

subsections.title: What Foodlink actually does: three businesses

blocks.text: Foodlink describes itself as a global luxury food services business with three lines: (i) Events Catering, which provides luxury catering for weddings, sports, social and corporate events in India and abroad; (ii) Casual Dining Restaurants & Cloud Kitchens in Indian metros and the UAE; and (iii) Banquets and Integrated F&B Services, run through three 'Jade Banquets' in Mumbai, Ahmedabad and New Delhi plus exclusive F&B mandates at third-party venues (S2). Under Ind AS 108 the company reports a single segment, hospitality, so the three-way split below is a management KPI rather than audited segment data (S1, S2).

blocks.caption: Revenue mix by business (Rs million; share of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: The economics differ sharply across the three. Events Catering is order-by-order work. The RHP says it is the largest revenue line and is exposed to swings in wedding demand, and that the company relies mainly on word of mouth from existing customers to win new ones (S1). Key catering customers named in the RHP are film actors, cricketers' families, HNIs, large corporates and certain government entities (S2). Banquets add a fixed venue base with recurring events: 1,089 events were catered in company-operated banquets and integrated F&B venues in FY26, against 1,092 events in the outdoor catering business (S2). Restaurants are the weakest and most volatile line, run under the India Bistro, China Bistro, Art of Dum and Glocal brands (S1, S12).

In H1 FY27 Events Catering fell to 44.15% of revenue, from 52.89% in FY26. This partly reflects seasonality, since the RHP says wedding catering peaks around a handful of auspicious months, and partly the restaurant and banquet lines growing (S1, S2).

Operations run on a hub-and-spoke model. Six centralised kitchens in India (Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Mohali, Hyderabad, Jaipur and New Delhi) and one in Dubai prepare food for all three businesses. Together they cover over 91,500 sq ft and can produce more than 100,000 meals a day (S1). Three storage facilities in Mumbai and three in Dubai hold cooking equipment for outdoor events (S1). The Jaipur kitchen began operating in FY27, and the RHP shows Rs 6.61 crore spent on opening kitchens in H1 FY27 (S1).

blocks.caption: Operating KPIs
rows: Events in banquets / integrated F&B venues

blocks.text: As of the RHP date the company runs 28 casual dining restaurants and cloud kitchens: 15 in India and 13 in the UAE (S2). It has operations in India, the UAE, the UK and Malaysia, and has catered events in countries including Switzerland, Turkey, Italy, Spain, France, Qatar, Thailand and the Maldives (S2). Every property, including the registered office, is leased (S2). Lease liabilities were Rs 97.10 crore at 30 September 2026, more than four times bank borrowings (S1).

On the supply side the company has no long-term agreement with any raw-material supplier. Inputs come from multiple suppliers, food wholesalers and distributors under annually renewed fixed-price contracts (S1, S16). Supplier concentration is low: the top 10 suppliers made up 19.80% of material costs in H1 FY27 (S16). The binding constraint is people, not raw materials. The group had 1,481 permanent employees at 30 September 2026, 533 of them in events catering, and permanent-staff attrition of 51.20% in FY26 and 49.50% in FY25 (S1).

The abridged prospectus marks revenue concentration among the top five customers as 'not applicable' (S2). That fits a business serving many one-off weddings and events, so customer concentration is not the risk here. The real concentrations are in event type (weddings), season, and Indian locations served by its kitchens (S1).

items: Foodlink Global Limited (Dubai) is an intermediate holding company in a tax-exempt zone. It does not run operations and generated no standalone revenue in the reported periods (S1).

Foodlink Global Restaurants & Catering Services LLC (FGRCS, UAE) is the material operating subsidiary for the UAE restaurants and catering. It earned Rs 125.26 million in FY25, lost Rs 14.27 million in FY26 and lost Rs 227.03 million in H1 FY27 (S1).
Mumbai Desi Adda Restaurant LLC (UAE) was acquired in Q4 FY25 and lost Rs 12.18 million in FY26 and Rs 3.92 million in H1 FY27 (S1).
Malaysian and UK step-down entities support the exclusive venue F&B mandates, including a waterfront convention venue in Penang (S1, S2).

blocks.text: The parent made a standalone profit of Rs 37.43 million in H1 FY27, while the group lost Rs 161.50 million. The UAE arm turned the result. That is the arm the IPO proceeds will fund for new restaurants (S1).

subsections.title: Market size and growth (company-commissioned F&S report)

blocks.text: All industry data in the RHP comes from a Frost & Sullivan report that Foodlink commissioned and paid for specifically for this offer (S1). By that report, the Indian foodservice market grows from Rs 8,314.30 billion in FY26 to Rs 12,887.30 billion in FY30. Total catering is Rs 2,626.3 billion in FY26, of which organised catering is Rs 1,602.0 billion, projected to reach Rs 2,835.2 billion by FY30 at about 15% CAGR (S2).

The F&S report is candid about catering's structural problems. Weddings drive 70-80% of organised catering revenue and bookings cluster around a few auspicious months. Shifts in sentiment can leave operators with high fixed costs and 15-25% menu wastage. Typical catering margins are said to hover in the single digits (S1). On banquets, the report notes the rise of micro-weddings and up to 30% idle capacity outside prime weekend dates (S1). These are the same pressures visible in Foodlink's H1 FY27 numbers.

The RHP concedes that there are 'currently no directly comparable listed entities' for its integrated catering, banquets and restaurants model (S1). The listed reference set is the QSR franchisees (Devyani, Jubilant FoodWorks, Sapphire, Restaurant Brands Asia, Westlife) plus Speciality Restaurants (S1, S16). None of them competes with Foodlink in luxury wedding catering. The relevant competitors are unlisted: Catering Collective (formerly Kapco Banquets), Elior India and Travel Food Services' catering arm, along with a long tail of regional and boutique wedding caterers (S1).

blocks.caption: Unlisted catering and hospitality peers per F&S (revenue from operations, Rs million)

blocks.text: Within this set Foodlink is profitable while its catering peers are close to breakeven or loss-making, a genuine point in its favour (S1). But the 'largest' claim needs context. It compares Foodlink's catering revenue with the total revenue of a chosen handful of unlisted companies, one of which (SkyGate, the Biryani By Kilo operator) is not a luxury caterer at all (S1). F&S also notes that the organised catering market alone is Rs 1,602 billion (S2). Foodlink's Rs 300 crore (Rs 3,001.28 million) of FY26 catering revenue is a fraction of one percent of that pool (S2).

Foodlink has no structural moat in the sense this report uses: no regulatory licence barrier, no import-substitution position, no proprietary technology and no long-term contracts. What it does have is brand and reputation in ultra-luxury weddings, built by the founder over three decades. That includes high-profile celebrity weddings and repeat HNI and corporate clients (S1, S2). The centralised-kitchen network lets it cater consistently across several cities, which the RHP presents as its main differentiator. Large unorganised caterers find that harder to replicate (S1).

items: Reputation moats in catering are perishable. They depend on chefs and execution teams, and Foodlink's permanent-staff attrition of around 50% a year shows how hard that talent is to keep (S1).
Pricing power is untested. The RHP gives no price or ticket-size data, and peers' margins show the category is structurally thin (S1).
The restaurant brands are not a moat. 21 outlets closed for low footfall in about three and a half years (S1).

Intellectual property is still being secured. 54 trademark applications are pending in India and eight abroad, and some marks are still being transferred from the promoter-linked Foodlink Services (India) Pvt Ltd (S1).

blocks.text: Plainly: this is a well-known brand in a fragmented, seasonal, labour-intensive service business. Leadership rests on a company-commissioned ranking in a narrowly defined niche, not on any barrier that stops a well-funded rival or a star chef-led boutique from taking clients.

subsections.title: Three-year restated P&L plus H1 FY27

blocks.text: Revenue grew 19.5% in FY25 and 25.9% in FY26, and EBITDA margin rose from 8.12% to about 13.7-13.8%. FY26 was the strongest year on record (S1, S2). Below EBITDA, the numbers are less clean. Depreciation and amortisation of about Rs 41 crore a year, much of it right-of-use lease amortisation, and finance costs that are mostly lease interest (Rs 9.72 crore of the Rs 13.18 crore in FY26) absorb most of the operating profit (S1). FY25 and FY26 profit also benefited from net tax credits, so reported PAT exceeded PBT in FY25. FY26 PBT was after a Rs 10.71 million exceptional charge (S1).

H1 FY27 reverses the trend. Revenue was Rs 219.8 crore for six months, EBITDA margin fell to 7.35%, and employee costs jumped to 27.85% of total income from 20.35% in FY26. The group recorded a Rs 16.15 crore loss (S1, S2). The RHP attributes the UAE subsidiary's H1 loss to 'heightened geopolitical tensions including the ongoing conflicts in the region' plus the normal seasonal slowdown (S1). The RHP provides no H1 FY26 comparison in the sections reviewed, so seasonality cannot be cleanly separated from deterioration.

subsections.title: Balance sheet health and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs million)

blocks.text: Bank leverage is low. Total borrowings of Rs 22.38 crore are 0.10x equity, and the debt-repayment object of Rs 21 crore would eliminate most of it (S1). The real fixed obligation is leases: about Rs 97 crore of lease liabilities on leased kitchens, banquets and restaurants. These behave like debt in a downturn (S1). Credit ratings are modest. India Ratings rated bank facilities IND BBB+/Stable/IND A2+ in August 2026, and CareEdge had CARE BBB/Stable in July 2024 (S1).

Net worth more than doubled in FY26, from Rs 106.22 crore to Rs 229.35 crore. FY26 PAT explains only Rs 29 crore of that. The Rs 47.21 crore financing inflow in FY26, in a year when borrowings fell, points to a fresh equity raise before the IPO. That is our inference from the cash flow statement, not a figure we confirmed in the RHP's capital-structure section (S1, S2).

items: Cash conversion weakened in FY26. Operating cash flow was 38% of EBITDA (Rs 29.91 crore vs Rs 78.43 crore), against about 72-76% in FY24-FY25 (S2).

Trade receivables roughly doubled, from Rs 29.84 crore to Rs 60.05 crore in FY26, on 26% revenue growth. That is about 39 days of revenue versus about 24 days in FY25, on our calculation from restated figures (S1).
The tax line flatters reported profit. There were net tax credits in FY24-FY26, and current tax in FY26 was only Rs 1.24 crore on Rs 29 crore PBT (S1).

Two of the four reported periods (FY24 and H1 FY27) are consolidated losses. The parent made a standalone loss of Rs 18.46 crore in FY24, which the RHP links to the Hyderabad kitchen launch, a Delhi convention-venue partnership and new outlets (S1).
The auditors include emphasis-of-matter paragraphs for the income-tax search (FY26 and H1 FY27) and the August 2023 GST search (FY24 and FY25) (S1).

blocks.text: The growth story (Rs 377 crore to Rs 567 crore revenue in two years) is real at the top line. But one strong year (FY26) is bracketed by losses on both sides, cash conversion fell in that strong year, and the latest half is a loss. The record does not yet show a business that compounds profit reliably.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key terms
rows: 26-30 November 2026; allotment 1 Dec; listing 3 Dec 2026 (BSE, NSE), tentative
1,88,87,738 shares, about Rs 360.76 crore at the upper band
88,35,382 shares, about Rs 168.76 crore at the upper band
Equirus Capital, JM Financial / MUFG Intime India

blocks.text: Sources for the terms above: S2, S4, S5 and S7. The fresh issue is Rs 192 crore, against Rs 160 crore in the June 2025 DRHP (S12). The company accounts for 75% QIB reservation because it does not meet the profitability track-record test of Regulation 6(1) and comes under Regulation 6(2) of SEBI ICDR. Under 6(2), at least 75% must go to QIBs and retail is capped at 10% (S2).

About 47% of the issue (Rs 168.76 crore) is an offer for sale. That money goes to selling shareholders, not the company. The promoter's weighted average acquisition cost is Rs 0.19 per share and Trans Global Hotels LLP's is Rs 0.24. Most private investors bought at about Rs 75.5, and Arpit Khandelwal at Rs 102.93 (S2).

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (Rs million) and deployment schedule
rows: Capex: one proposed centralised kitchen (Rajasthan, possibly Udaipur)
Capex: two proposed banquets (Rajasthan and Bengaluru)
Investment in FGRCS (UAE) for four casual dining restaurants (1 China Bistro, 3 Art of Dum, in Abu Dhabi and Dubai)
Up to 25% of gross fresh proceeds; to be fixed at pricing

blocks.text: Of the Rs 192 crore fresh issue, about Rs 113.7 crore (59%) is earmarked for capex, all scheduled for FY28. Rs 21 crore goes to debt repayment in FY27, and the remaining about Rs 57.3 crore covers general corporate purposes and issue expenses (S1, S5). The objects have not been appraised by any bank or financial institution, and a monitoring agency will oversee deployment (S1).

items: No property has been identified, and no lease signed, for the kitchen, banquets or UAE restaurants. Lease deposits and rent will come from internal accruals or debt, not IPO money (S1).
No capex orders have been placed. Costs rest on vendor quotations, with no definitive agreements (S1).
Location-specific approvals (FSSAI, fire, trade licences, music licence) cannot be applied for until sites are found (S1).

The single kitchen is budgeted at Rs 21.40 crore for an assumed 10,000 sq ft. The company spent Rs 6.61 crore opening its Jaipur kitchen in H1 FY27, so the budget looks generous and deserves scrutiny (S1).
The upstox day-1 article describes the UAE object as 'two' restaurants. The RHP says four, and we rely on the RHP (S1, S8).

subsections.title: What the money does for shareholders

blocks.text: The largest single use, Rs 50.81 crore, funds the restaurant format with the worst record (21 closures since April 2023), in the geography that produced a Rs 22.70 crore H1 loss, at sites not yet chosen (S1). The banquet and kitchen spend in Rajasthan and Bengaluru follows the better-performing banquets line and the wedding-destination thesis, and is easier to defend (S1). Debt repayment is sensible but small (S1).
Net: less than half the issue funds the company, and most of the part that does is a forward-looking bet with no sites, orders or approvals in place, deploying in FY28.

Selling shareholders include the promoter Sanjay Vazirani (22,86,446 shares, about Rs 43.67 crore), promoter-group members Trans Global Hotels LLP and Ankita Chugh, and long-standing financial investors: Arpit Khandelwal (Plutus), V'Ocean, Oaks Asset Management, Aarkay, the Welspun Group Master Trust, Aarin Capital (T.V. Mohandas Pai and Ranjan Pai) and Bona Terra (S2, S4). Early-stage investors exiting through an IPO is normal. The promoter also selling at a tiny cost base while the company posts an H1 loss is not a supportive signal.

The sole promoter is founder, Chairman and MD Sanjay Manohar Vazirani. He has a hotel-management diploma from IHM Mumbai and more than three decades in luxury catering and F&B in India and the UAE. Earlier he worked at Holiday Inn, Peninsula Restaurant and The Basement, and he was proprietor of Hotel Aid (S2). Foodlink as a brand dates to 2003 (S15). The listed company was incorporated in 2015 and later absorbed the catering and restaurant businesses through a scheme of arrangement (S1). His experience is genuinely relevant to the domain. He has no record of running a listed company.

blocks.caption: Board and KMP
rows: 49.50% pre-offer; FY26 pay Rs 28.88 million, paid by UAE subsidiary FGRCS; entitled to 5% commission on earnings before tax
20+ years in F&B; COO at Foodlink Services (India) since 2006; Rs 16.0 million p.a.

blocks.text: Sources for the table: S1 and S2. All three independent directors joined on 12 June 2025, about two weeks before the DRHP was filed, so the board's independent oversight is recent (S1). Some of the outside affiliations are mildly awkward. The Oaks nominee director sits on the board of Wow Momo Foods, which Foodlink is suing for trademark infringement ('WOW! CHINA BISTRO'). One independent director, through IL&FS Engineering & Construction, is a respondent in an SFIO criminal complaint over disclosures. These relate to other companies, but they belong in the record (S1).

items: Rent to Foodlink Services (India) Pvt Ltd, a promoter-influenced entity, was Rs 15.23 million in FY26 and Rs 7.62 million in H1 FY27, plus a Rs 2.22 million security deposit. Some trademarks are still being transferred from this entity (S1).
Rent to the promoter personally was Rs 3.23 million in FY26, and expense reimbursements to him were Rs 9.67 million in FY26 (S1).

Ankita Chugh Weddings & Events Pvt Ltd, linked to promoter-group shareholder and former director Ankita Chugh, paid banquet renting income of Rs 8.14 million in FY25. Nothing is recorded in FY26 or H1 FY27 (S1).
The promoter personally guarantees some borrowings, Rs 18.09 crore outstanding at 30 September 2026 per one secondary RHP summary (S16).
Managerial pay is the largest RPT component: promoter Rs 28.88 million and Priya Gogte Rs 12.17 million in FY26 (S1).

blocks.text: The RPT section is broadly routine at under about 2% of revenue. The only structural point is that operating premises and brand IP still partly sit with promoter-linked Foodlink Services (India). That is worth tracking, but it is not a red flag on its own.

Income-tax search. A search and seizure under section 132 of the Income-tax Act began on 17 December 2025 at premises associated with the company, and Rs 10.59 million in cash was seized. A section 158BC notice dated 5 June 2026 opened a block assessment for 1 April 2019 to 13 February 2026. No order had been issued by the RHP date, and the auditors flag the search as an emphasis of matter (S1). The potential liability is unquantified. This is the single biggest governance unknown in the issue.

items: Older income-tax dispute (AY2017-18/18-19). The assessing officer added Rs 104.46 million under section 68 for share capital and premium, and Rs 28.06 million for cash deposited during demonetisation. Both were deleted by CIT(A) and upheld by ITAT. The department's appeal at the Bombay High Court is pending, with a disputed claim of Rs 109.67 million (S1, S17).

GST. A search in August 2023 was followed by provisional attachment of bank accounts in 2024 (since lifted). A show-cause notice of 17 April 2026 alleges non-payment of Rs 233.16 million. A demand of Rs 4.07 million plus equal interest and penalty was confirmed in May 2026, and the company has appealed (S1).
ESIC. An arrears order of Rs 3.62 million covers the predecessor restaurant entity and the promoter. A stay is in place with 15% deposited (S1).
The aggregate quantifiable amount against the company is Rs 154.78 million across 11 tax matters, one regulatory and two material civil cases (S2).

Pending approvals include health trade licences for the Delhi and Jaipur kitchens and the Delhi banquet, fire NOCs for the Mohali and Delhi kitchens, and the ISO 22000 renewal, which has been delayed (S1).

Execution risk on proceeds. No sites, leases, orders or approvals exist for the kitchen, banquets or UAE restaurants. Delays or cost overruns fall on shareholders, and any shortfall is funded from internal accruals (S1).

UAE exposure. FGRCS turned from a Rs 125.26 million profit in FY25 to a Rs 227.03 million loss in H1 FY27. The RHP cites ongoing regional conflict, cancelled or postponed orders and weaker discretionary spending. Rs 50.81 crore of fresh money still goes there (S1).
Restaurant track record. The company closed 2 restaurants and 2 cloud kitchens in FY24, 5 and 6 in FY25, and 4 and 2 in H1 FY27 for low footfall, yet plans more restaurants with IPO money (S1).
Concentration in wedding catering. Events Catering was 52.89% of FY26 revenue, and the business depends on luxury wedding demand, auspicious-date calendars and word-of-mouth referrals (S1).

blocks.text: These four risks feed each other. An H1 loss, a UAE-heavy use of proceeds and a seasonal core business together make the next 12-18 months unusually binary for a consumer-services IPO (S1).

items: Tax overhang. The block assessment after the December 2025 search has no order yet. A GST show-cause notice of Rs 233.16 million and the Rs 109.67 million income-tax appeal at the High Court are also pending (S1).
Earnings quality and cash conversion. FY26 operating cash flow was 38% of EBITDA, receivables doubled, and reported PAT depended on tax credits (S1, S2).
Labour intensity and attrition. Permanent-staff attrition was 51.20% in FY26 and 23.08% in H1 FY27 (not annualised). Service quality is the product (S1).
Licence dependence. Several approvals are pending. Liquor at China Bistro, Kamala Mills runs on the property owner's licence, and event music and liquor licences sit with third parties (S1).
Fixed lease burden. Lease liabilities of about Rs 97 crore against seasonal, discretionary revenue add operating leverage on the way down (S1).

blocks.text: Not material, in our view: customer concentration (no top-5 dependence disclosed), supplier concentration (top 10 suppliers about 20% of material costs) and bank debt, which is small and largely repaid from proceeds (S2, S16).

subsections.title: What the RHP says management will do

blocks.text: The RHP's stated strategies are qualitative. Expand Events Catering into newer geographies with more focus on sports and corporate events. Expand casual dining and cloud kitchens 'on an asset light model'. Widen the banquets and integrated F&B footprint (S2). The only dated plan is the deployment schedule: debt repayment in FY27, and the Rajasthan kitchen, two banquets and four UAE restaurants in FY28 (S1). The board approved the funding requirement on 10 November 2026, based on internal estimates and vendor quotations (S1).

We found no IPO-period investor call, guidance or interview giving revenue or margin targets. As is normal, the RHP gives no numeric forecast. Search results did not surface a management interview from the issue period (S1, S18).
There is a contradiction to note. The strategy says casual dining will grow 'asset light', yet the largest object is Rs 50.81 crore of capex for company-built UAE restaurants (S1, S2).

In November 2021, at its $8 million Series B led by Arpit Khandelwal, the founder put the FY22 revenue run-rate at Rs 100 crore and targeted about Rs 300 crore by FY23-FY24 (S15). FY24 revenue came in at Rs 377.19 crore, so that target was met (S2).

In July 2023 the founder targeted Rs 800-1,000 crore revenue in 3-4 years. He also planned to grow restaurants from 35 to 100 across India in three years, with Rs 400-500 crore of investment funded mostly from internal accruals, and set an IPO 'in next couple of years' (S14). Three years later the company has 17 casual dining restaurants and 11 cloud kitchens, and FY26 revenue of Rs 567.50 crore (S2). The restaurant ambition clearly missed, and the revenue target now needs roughly 40-75% growth from FY26 in about a year.

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 bids and grey market (partial, day 1)

blocks.text: Anchor book. On 25 November 2026 the company raised Rs 162.34 crore from anchors: 84,99,483 shares at Rs 191 (S4, S7). By category the anchor book was FPI 33.58%, AIF 27.10%, mutual funds 16.94%, FVC 16.63% and NBFC 5.75% (S4). Named anchors include Amicorp Capital (Mauritius), ITI Mutual Fund (Small Cap and Flexi Cap funds), Founders Collective Fund, SG Finserve, Svan Velocity Fund, Shine Star Build-Cap, Meru Investment Fund PCC Cell 1 and Cognizant Capital Dynamic Opportunities Fund (S7, S8). Lock-in runs to 31 December 2026 for 50% of anchor shares and to 1 March 2027 for the rest (S4). Only one mainstream domestic mutual fund house is named. The rest are mostly smaller AIFs and offshore vehicles.

blocks.caption: Day-1 intraday snapshots, 26 Nov 2026 (partial; issue closes 30 Nov)

blocks.text: Sources for the table: S9, S19, S10 and S11. These are morning snapshots from the first of three bidding days. They differ by source and time, and none is an end-of-day figure. QIB bids typically arrive on the last day, so the QIB 0.00x readings say nothing yet. Day-1 demand is retail-led and modest.

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): ipoguru and ipomarket both showed Rs 16 on the morning of 26 November 2026, down from a Rs 21 peak on 24 November. Chanakya Nipothi showed Rs 18 (S6, S10, S11). This is not an investment signal and plays no part in our verdict. Business Standard reports that brokerages are divided on the issue (S18).

method: The primary source is the full Red Herring Prospectus dated 19 November 2026 (S1), hosted by BRLM Equirus, together with SEBI's abridged prospectus (S2, S3). We read both directly: the risk factors, objects of the offer and deployment schedule, F&S industry peer benchmarking, management, related-party note 40, capitalisation, financial indebtedness, MD&A results of operations and outstanding litigation. We did not read the original June 2025 DRHP; its terms come from news coverage (S12, S13). Issue terms, anchor book and lock-ins were cross-checked across Chittorgarh, Zerodha, Kotak Neo and Upstox. One preview (S6) earlier quoted a tentative Rs 180-191 band; the final Rs 181-191 band is confirmed by S4, S5 and S7. Some secondary pages carry errors that we resolved in favour of the RHP: Chittorgarh's borrowing column is misaligned, Kotak gives Sep-26 borrowings as Rs 25.3 crore against Rs 22.38 crore in the RHP, and Upstox gives the UAE restaurant count as two against four in the RHP. The promoter guarantee figure (S16) and the RPT share of revenue were not independently verified beyond the noted pages. The pre-IPO equity raise behind the FY26 jump in net worth is our inference from the cash flow statement. Subscription data are partial intraday day-1 snapshots from different sources and times. Several commentary sites (Substack analyses, IndiaTV, the full Business Standard article) returned 403/402 errors and were not used beyond search-result titles. Grey market figures come from tracker sites, are unofficial and were not used in the verdict. Valuation was deliberately excluded per the brief. Rupee crore figures are converted from the RHP's Rs million (10 million = 1 crore).
